edited_rows.rationale: The psalm opens with the verse-initial hodu-le-YHWH call: “Give thanks to Yahweh!” (web:Ps.105.1), with the Hebrew 'הוֹד֣וּ לַ֭יהוָה' at oshb:Ps.105.1, a tier-1 opener device (psalm_device_inventory.json hodu_openings). The imperative cluster continues: “Call on his name” (web:Ps.105.1), “Sing to him, sing praises to him” (web:Ps.105.2), “Glory in his holy name” (web:Ps.105.3), “Seek Yahweh and his strength” (web:Ps.105.4), and also “Remember his marvelous works” (web:Ps.105.5), before the unit closes addressing “you offspring of Abraham… you children of Jacob, his chosen ones” (web:Ps.105.6), naming the addressees the historical recital that follows will retell.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Closing the unit at 105:5 (its final imperative) and giving the vocative “offspring of Abraham” (web:Ps.105.6) its own row was considered, but 105:6 is the vocative addressee of 105:5’s “remember,” not its grammatical object, so splitting it would sever the imperative from its addressee.
observed_substrate_signals: verse-initial hodu-le-YHWH opener ('הוֹד֣וּ לַ֭יהוָה', 105:1, oshb:Ps.105.1), tier-1 device per the frame inventory
sustained imperative-cluster mode runs 105:1-6 (give thanks, call, sing, glory, seek, remember), closing on the vocative addressee it governs
edited_rows.device_notes: Psalm 105 coheres as one composition — parent grouping Psalm 105; every row below shares that single parent. The historical recital moves covenant → Joseph → Egypt/plagues → exodus → settlement across the rows that follow.

edited_rows.rationale: A declarative statement opens the unit with its own independent pronoun: “He is Yahweh, our God” (web:Ps.105.7) — the Hebrew reads 'ה֭וּא יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֵ֑ינוּ' (oshb:Ps.105.7) — turning from the imperative calls of 105:1-6 to covenant declaration. “He has remembered his covenant forever” (web:Ps.105.8) names “the covenant which he made with Abraham, his oath to Isaac” (web:Ps.105.9), matching 'לְיִשְׂחָֽק' at oshb:Ps.105.9, confirmed “to Jacob… to Israel” (web:Ps.105.10), and closes with the land grant quoted in direct speech: “To you I will give the land of Canaan, the lot of your inheritance” (web:Ps.105.11).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Closing the unit at 105:10 and giving the quoted land grant (105:11) its own row was considered, but 105:11’s “saying” clause is the direct object of 105:8-10’s covenant-remembering, not a new speech act beginning a fresh unit.
observed_substrate_signals: independent-pronoun declaration 'ה֭וּא' opens the unit (105:7, oshb:Ps.105.7), a subject-class shift from the imperative mode of 105:1-6
covenant chain runs patriarch-by-patriarch (Abraham 105:9, Jacob/Israel 105:10) to its quoted land-grant close (105:11)
edited_rows.device_notes: The oath “to Isaac” (web:Ps.105.9) at 105:9 is spelled 'לְיִשְׂחָֽק' (oshb:Ps.105.9) with sin rather than the standard tzade; a skeleton sweep of the lamed-prefixed spelling as quoted ('לישחק') returns 1 verse book-wide (105:9 only), while a skeleton sweep of the bare-root spelling (ישחק, lamed stripped) returns 4 verses book-wide (Ps.2.4, Ps.37.13, Ps.52.6, Ps.105.9) — the other three are the common verb 'he will laugh' (root s-h-q), a consonantal homograph found elsewhere in the Psalter; a skeleton sweep for the standard tzade spelling returns 0 verses book-wide, so 105:9 is the Psalter’s one occurrence of Isaac’s name, and it carries the alternate spelling.

edited_rows.rationale: A temporal clause opens the narrative proper: “when they were but a few men in number” (web:Ps.105.12), whose Hebrew is 'בִּֽ֭הְיוֹתָם מְתֵ֣י מִסְפָּ֑ר' (oshb:Ps.105.12), shifting from covenant declaration to the patriarchs’ own wandering. “They went about from nation to nation” (web:Ps.105.13) and Yahweh “reproved kings for their sakes” (web:Ps.105.14), closing on the quoted royal warning: “Don't touch my anointed ones! Do my prophets no harm!” (web:Ps.105.15), rendering 'אַֽל תִּגְּע֥וּ בִמְשִׁיחָ֑י' (oshb:Ps.105.15).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Extending the unit through 105:16 was considered, but 105:16 opens with a wayyiqtol narrative verb ('וַיִּקְרָ֣א', roughly 'and he called,' oshb:Ps.105.16) beginning the famine that triggers the Joseph narrative, a new narrative-sequence link rather than a continuation of the royal-protection material.
observed_substrate_signals: temporal clause 'בִּֽ֭הְיוֹתָם' opens the unit (105:12, oshb:Ps.105.12), a narrative-time shift into the patriarchal period
unit closes on quoted divine speech protecting “my anointed ones” / “my prophets” (105:15, web:Ps.105.15)

edited_rows.rationale: A wayyiqtol narrative verb opens the Joseph story: “He called for a famine on the land” (web:Ps.105.16), collated to 'וַיִּקְרָ֣א רָ֭עָב' (oshb:Ps.105.16). “He sent a man before them. Joseph was sold for a slave” (web:Ps.105.17), set against 'יוֹסֵֽף' (oshb:Ps.105.17), his feet bruised “with shackles” (web:Ps.105.18) until “Yahweh's word proved him true” (web:Ps.105.19), the king’s release of him (web:Ps.105.20), his rule over the royal house (web:Ps.105.21), and the unit closes with Joseph’s authority “to discipline his princes… and to teach his elders wisdom” (web:Ps.105.22).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting Joseph’s imprisonment (105:17-19) from his exaltation (105:20-22) as two rows was considered, but both develop one reversal-of-fortune narrative arc, with no wayyiqtol restart marking a break before 105:23; the arc runs to its close at 105:22, and only the wayyiqtol at 105:23 opens the next unit, corporate Israel’s entry into Egypt.
observed_substrate_signals: wayyiqtol narrative verb 'וַיִּקְרָ֣א' opens the unit (105:16, oshb:Ps.105.16), narrative-sequence link distinct from the temporal clause of 105:12

the reversal-of-fortune arc (enslaved, tested, then exalted) runs unbroken from Joseph’s sale (105:17) through his rule (105:20-22), with no wayyiqtol restart marking a break until 105:23 opens the next unit
edited_rows.device_notes: A ketiv/qere note sits at oshb:Ps.105.18 (pmarks_Ps.json kq) on the word rendered “his feet” (web:Ps.105.18) / 'his foot'; not quoted here, disclosed because the span crosses it.

edited_rows.rationale: A new wayyiqtol verb introduces a new named subject: “Israel also came into Egypt” (web:Ps.105.23) — MT reads 'וַיָּבֹ֣א יִשְׂרָאֵ֣ל מִצְרָ֑יִם' (oshb:Ps.105.23) — turning from Joseph individually to Israel corporately. “He increased his people greatly” (web:Ps.105.24) and “turned their heart to hate his people” (web:Ps.105.25) set up the oppression that “He sent Moses, his servant, and Aaron” answers (web:Ps.105.26), the Hebrew 'שָׁ֭לַח מֹשֶׁ֣ה עַבְדּ֑וֹ' at oshb:Ps.105.26; the unit closes with Moses and Aaron performing “miracles among them, and wonders in the land of Ham” (web:Ps.105.27), the general statement the plague catalogue itemizes from 105:28.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Extending the unit through the whole nine-verse plague list was considered, but 105:28 opens the itemized catalogue proper with its own perfect verb ('שָׁ֣לַֽח', roughly 'he sent [darkness],' oshb:Ps.105.28 — a ketiv/qere note sits later in this verse per pmarks_Ps.json kq, not quoted here), where 105:27 still speaks in the general terms (“miracles… wonders”, web:Ps.105.27) that the catalogue then specifies.
observed_substrate_signals: new wayyiqtol verb with new named subject Israel opens the unit (105:23), narrative-subject shift from Joseph
unit runs population growth → oppression → the sending of Moses/Aaron → a general miracles/wonders statement that the following catalogue itemizes
edited_rows.device_notes: The plague sequence itemized from 105:28 (darkness, blood, frogs, insects, hail, locusts, and the death of the “firstborn”) covers 7 of the traditional plagues and omits the livestock-pestilence and boils material present in this psalm's own catalogue by their absence; a cross-book relation to Exodus’s narrative noted as texture, not boundary authority for these rows.

edited_rows.rationale: The plague catalogue opens: “He sent darkness, and made it dark” (web:Ps.105.28); the Hebrew 'שָׁ֣לַֽח חֹ֭שֶׁךְ' underlies it at oshb:Ps.105.28 (a ketiv/qere note sits later in this verse per pmarks_Ps.json kq, not quoted here), opening a plague disruption group: waters “turned… into blood” killing the fish (web:Ps.105.29), the land “swarmed with frogs, even in the rooms of their kings” (web:Ps.105.30), and “swarms of flies… and lice in all their borders” (web:Ps.105.31), which closes the group before the destruction-class plagues open at 105:32.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Treating the full plague list as one nine-verse unit was considered as the more conservative reading of one unbroken catalogue, but the darkness/blood/frogs/insects group (105:28-31) is closed by “all their borders” (web:Ps.105.31), while the hail/locusts/“firstborn” group that follows escalates toward the climactic strike — the split is a content grouping inside one catalogue, not a strong grammatical break, and is held at medium confidence for that reason.
observed_substrate_signals: disruption group opens with 'שָׁ֣לַֽח חֹ֭שֶׁךְ' (105:28, oshb:Ps.105.28; a ketiv/qere note sits later in this verse per pmarks_Ps.json kq, not quoted here), spanning 4 verses (105:28-31) but 5 plague nouns under 4 verbs, since 105:31 carries two nouns (arov, kinnim) under one verb (vayavo)

group closes on the summarizing phrase “all their borders” (105:31, web:Ps.105.31); the verb pattern is unbroken across five consecutive waw-less 3ms openers (105:28-32, oshb:Ps.105.28-Ps.105.32); the first waw-initial opener in the catalogue is 105:33 (oshb:Ps.105.33), making 105:32|33 the byte-true rival seam, so the 105:31|32 split stands only as a content grouping, not a grammatical break
the two-word opening formula 'אָ֭מַר וַיָּבֹ֣א' recurs byte-identically at 105:31 and 105:34 (oshb:Ps.105.31, oshb:Ps.105.34), a continuity signal straddling the 105:31|32 boundary

edited_rows.rationale: The destruction-class plagues open: “He gave them hail for rain, with lightning in their land” (web:Ps.105.32), in Hebrew 'נָתַ֣ן גִּשְׁמֵיהֶ֣ם' (oshb:Ps.105.32), striking “their vines and also their fig trees” (web:Ps.105.33). Locusts follow “without number” (web:Ps.105.34), eating “every plant in their land” (web:Ps.105.35), and the catalogue climaxes with the “firstborn” struck: “He struck also all the firstborn in their land” (web:Ps.105.36), with the Hebrew 'וַיַּ֣ךְ כָּל בְּכ֣וֹר' at oshb:Ps.105.36, closing the plague sequence before the exodus departure opens at 105:37.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Closing the unit at 105:35 and giving the “firstborn” strike its own one-verse row was considered, but 105:36 opens with its own wayyiqtol verb ('וַיַּ֣ךְ', 'and he struck,' oshb:Ps.105.36) continuing the same destruction sequence as its capstone rather than opening an independent unit.
observed_substrate_signals: hail/locust/“firstborn” destruction group opens with 'נָתַ֣ן גִּשְׁמֵיהֶ֣ם' (105:32, oshb:Ps.105.32); the verb pattern is unbroken across five consecutive waw-less 3ms openers (105:28-32, oshb:Ps.105.28-Ps.105.32); the first waw-initial opener in the catalogue is 105:33 (oshb:Ps.105.33), making 105:32|33 the byte-true rival seam, so the 105:31|32 split stands only as a content grouping, not a grammatical break
wayyiqtol 'וַיַּ֣ךְ' (oshb:Ps.105.36) at 105:36 continues the same sequence rather than marking a fresh start
the two-word opening formula 'אָ֭מַר וַיָּבֹ֣א' recurs byte-identically at 105:31 and 105:34 (oshb:Ps.105.31, oshb:Ps.105.34), a continuity signal straddling the 105:31|32 boundary

edited_rows.rationale: A causal clause returns explicitly to the psalm’s own covenant theme: “For he remembered his holy word” (web:Ps.105.42), matching 'כִּֽי זָ֭כַר אֶת דְּבַ֣ר קָדְשׁ֑וֹ' at oshb:Ps.105.42, echoing the covenant-memory language of 105:8-9. “He brought his people out with joy” (web:Ps.105.43) and “gave them the lands of the nations” (web:Ps.105.44) lead to the closing purpose clause — “that they might keep his statutes, and observe his laws” (web:Ps.105.45) — and the psalm ends with hallelu-Yah, whose Hebrew is 'הַֽלְלוּ יָֽהּ' (oshb:Ps.105.45).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the covenant-memory clause (105:42) from the closing purpose statement (105:43-45) as two rows was considered, but 105:42’s 'כִּֽי' clause is the causal ground for the whole closing movement ('he remembered his holy word, he brought his people out with joy, that they might keep his statutes'), one argument chain.
observed_substrate_signals: causal 'כִּֽי' clause opens the unit (105:42), a theological-register return to the covenant language of 105:8-9
unit closes on a purpose clause (105:45) plus the psalm-final hallelu-Yah, tier-1 closer device
edited_rows.device_notes: Psalm 105 closes with 'הַֽלְלוּ יָֽהּ' (oshb:Ps.105.45), matching Psalm 104’s own hallelu-Yah close; both sit inside the curated frame inventory’s 24 imperative-frame occurrences (11 verse-initial + 13 verse-final), with two skeleton-tier collisions disclosed separately (web:Ps.115.17 = oshb:Ps.115.17, a verbal collocation; web:Ps.22.27 = oshb:Ps.22.28, a full-divine-name collision). As texture, not evidence bearing on this row's own close.

edited_rows.rationale: The address shifts to a first-person singular petition: “Remember me, Yahweh, with the favor that you show to your people. Visit me with your salvation,” (web:Ps.106.4) opens on the imperative-plus-suffix זָכְרֵ֣נִי (oshb:Ps.106.4), 'remember me, Yahweh' — distinct in person from the plural hymn just closed. Three purpose clauses stack in the verse that follows, לִרְא֤וֹת … לִ֭שְׂמֹחַ … לְ֝הִתְהַלֵּ֗ל (oshb:Ps.106.5), “that I may see the prosperity of your chosen, that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation, that I may glory with your inheritance.” (web:Ps.106.5), before the voice returns to first-person plural at the confession that opens next.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Grouping 106:4-5 with the confession formula that follows as one row was considered, but the plea's singular voice gives way to the confession's plural voice at the verse boundary, a person-shift the tiling should respect.
observed_substrate_signals: a first-person singular imperative-suffix verb ('remember me') opens v4, a voice shift from the plural imperatives of v1
three infinitive-construct purpose clauses (le- prefix) stack across v5
the plural first-person voice returns at the next verse's confession formula

edited_rows.rationale: The confession formula that launches the historical recital stands alone: “We have sinned with our fathers. We have committed iniquity. We have done wickedly.” (web:Ps.106.6) stacks three plural perfect verbs, חָטָ֥אנוּ עִם אֲבוֹתֵ֗ינוּ הֶעֱוִ֥ינוּ הִרְשָֽׁעְנוּ (oshb:Ps.106.6), with no historical referent yet named — the recital's initial named episode, Egypt and the Red Sea, opens the verse immediately after.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Attaching 106:6 to the Egypt/Red Sea episode as its opening line was considered — the two verses share the byte-distinct but accent-stripped-identical catchword 'our fathers' (oshb:Ps.106.6, oshb:Ps.106.7) straddling this boundary — but the confession verbs of 106:6 name no place or event of their own, standing as a general formula the named recital then fills in rather than opening it.
observed_substrate_signals: three stacked plural perfect verbs ('we have sinned...committed iniquity...done wickedly') with no object or place-name, unlike the episodes that follow
the verse's voice shifts to first-person plural ('we') for the first time in the psalm — 106:4-5's petition is entirely first-person singular — a voice shift rather than a return
no proper name occurs in this verse, contrasting with the named settings that structure the recital from the next verse forward

edited_rows.rationale: The recital's initial episode narrates Egypt and the Red Sea: “Our fathers didn't understand your wonders in Egypt. They didn't remember the multitude of your loving kindnesses, but were rebellious at the sea, even at the Red Sea.” (web:Ps.106.7) names the setting, בְמִצְרַ֨יִם … עַל יָ֣ם בְּיַם סֽוּף (oshb:Ps.106.7), that the following verses develop — rescue for Yahweh's name's sake (web:Ps.106.8), the sea rebuked and dried, וַיִּגְעַ֣ר בְּיַם ס֭וּף וַֽיֶּחֱרָ֑ב (oshb:Ps.106.9), “He rebuked the Red Sea also, and it was dried up; so he led them through the depths, as through a desert.” (web:Ps.106.9), deliverance from the enemy's hand (web:Ps.106.10), the drowned adversaries (web:Ps.106.11), and the people's belief and song (web:Ps.106.12) — before the recital's next episode turns from the sea to the wilderness craving.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Ending this unit at 106:11 and giving 106:12's belief-and-song response its own row was considered, but the response completes the episode's own arc — rebellion at the sea, then rescue, then belief — rather than opening a new referent.
observed_substrate_signals: Egypt and the Red Sea are both named at v7, the recital's initial specific setting
the Red Sea name recurs at v9, a verbal echo of v7's naming within the same episode
the episode closes on a belief-and-song formula at v12, a different response-class from the 'forgot' formula that opens the next episode

the recital's opening word here ('our fathers', oshb:Ps.106.7) is accent_stripped/skeleton-identical to, but byte-distinct from, the 'our fathers' token closing the preceding verse (oshb:Ps.106.6), a catchword straddling this row's own opening seam

edited_rows.rationale: Named persons enter the recital: “They envied Moses also in the camp, and Aaron, Yahweh's saint.” (web:Ps.106.16) opens with Moses and Aaron named, לְ֭מֹשֶׁה … לְ֝אַהֲרֹ֗ן (oshb:Ps.106.16), then Dathan and Abiram named as the ground opens and swallows them, וַתִּבְלַ֣ע דָּתָ֑ן וַ֝תְּכַ֗ס עַל עֲדַ֥ת אֲבִירָֽם (oshb:Ps.106.17), “The earth opened and swallowed up Dathan, and covered the company of Abiram.” (web:Ps.106.17). The fire that burns the company closes the episode, “A fire was kindled in their company. The flame burned up the wicked.” (web:Ps.106.18), before the calf narrative opens with its own place name, Horeb.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Treating vv16-18 as a continuation of the craving episode rather than its own row was considered, but the shift to naming specific persons marks a distinct narrative unit from the unnamed craving-in-the-desert failure.
observed_substrate_signals: personal names Moses, Aaron, Dathan, and Abiram cluster across vv16-17, a naming density the craving episode (vv13-15) lacks entirely
a fire-consumes-the-wicked formula closes the episode at v18
the following episode opens on a place name, Horeb, rather than a person

edited_rows.rationale: The golden-calf episode opens on its own place name: “They made a calf in Horeb, and worshiped a molten image.” (web:Ps.106.19) — עֵ֥גֶל בְּחֹרֵ֑ב (oshb:Ps.106.19). The exchanged glory (web:Ps.106.20), the forgotten Savior who had worked wonders in Egypt and at the Red Sea (web:Ps.106.21-Ps.106.22, עַל יַם סֽוּף (oshb:Ps.106.22)), and Moses' own intercession close the episode: “Therefore he said that he would destroy them, had Moses, his chosen, not stood before him in the breach, to turn away his wrath, so that he wouldn't destroy them.” (web:Ps.106.23) — עָמַ֣ד בַּפֶּ֣רֶץ (oshb:Ps.106.23) — before the recital turns to the spies' rejection of the land.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the calf-worship narration (106:19-20) from the forgetting-and-intercession unit (106:21-23) into two rows was considered, but both share Horeb's episode, and Moses' intercession answers the same forgetting the unit itself narrates, with no independent referent break between them.
observed_substrate_signals: the place name Horeb opens the episode at v19, distinct from the Dathan/Abiram naming that precedes it
the Red Sea name recurs at v22, echoing its earlier naming at vv7 and 9 without reopening that episode
Moses named as intercessor ('stood in the breach') closes the episode at v23

edited_rows.rationale: The recital turns from Horeb to the promised land: “Yes, they despised the pleasant land. They didn't believe his word,” (web:Ps.106.24) — בְּאֶ֣רֶץ חֶמְדָּ֑ה (oshb:Ps.106.24). Murmuring against Yahweh's voice follows (web:Ps.106.25), then the sworn oath of judgment, “Therefore he swore to them that he would overthrow them in the wilderness,” (web:Ps.106.26) — וַיִּשָּׂ֣א יָד֣וֹ (oshb:Ps.106.26) — extended to scattering their offspring among the nations (web:Ps.106.27), before the recital names a new place, Baal Peor.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Attaching 106:24-27 to the preceding calf episode as one long wilderness-rebellion unit was considered, but the referent shifts from Horeb and the calf to the land itself, and the oath at v26 answers this episode's own despising rather than the calf's.
observed_substrate_signals: a 'pleasant/desirable land' phrase names the promised-land referent at v24, distinct from Horeb's calf-and-image referent
an oath formula ('lifted his hand', i.e. swore) opens the judgment at v26
the episode's offspring-scattering close carries no personal name, unlike the Baal Peor episode's Phinehas that follows

edited_rows.rationale: A new named place opens the episode: “They joined themselves also to Baal Peor, and ate the sacrifices of the dead.” (web:Ps.106.28) — לְבַ֣עַל פְּע֑וֹר (oshb:Ps.106.28) — followed by the plague (web:Ps.106.29) and Phinehas's own intervention: “Then Phinehas stood up and executed judgment, so the plague was stopped.” (web:Ps.106.30) — פִּֽ֭ינְחָס (oshb:Ps.106.30) — credited to him for righteousness across generations (web:Ps.106.31), a second named intercessor after Moses' stand at Horeb's aftermath, before the recital names its next place, Meribah.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Ending this unit at 106:29 and giving Phinehas's intervention (106:30-31) its own row was considered, but the plague's stopping and Phinehas's act are the same event described from two angles, not two episodes.
observed_substrate_signals: the place name Baal Peor opens the episode at v28, distinct from the land-despising episode that precedes it
the personal name Phinehas enters at v30 as the episode's own intercessor, paralleling Moses' intercession at v23 without repeating its vocabulary
a credited-for-righteousness formula closes the episode at v31 on covenant-legal language absent from the surrounding narrative verses

edited_rows.rationale: A fourth named place closes the recital's cluster of wilderness-rebellion sites: “They angered him also at the waters of Meribah, so that Moses was troubled for their sakes;” (web:Ps.106.32) — עַל מֵ֥י מְרִיבָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.106.32) — and the cause is named directly: “because they were rebellious against his spirit, he spoke rashly with his lips.” (web:Ps.106.33) — וַ֝יְבַטֵּ֗א בִּשְׂפָתָֽיו (oshb:Ps.106.33). Moses himself now suffers the consequence, a reversal from his intercessor's role at Horeb's aftermath (עָמַ֣ד בַּפֶּ֣רֶץ (oshb:Ps.106.23)).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Folding 106:32-33 into the Baal Peor unit as its closing pair was considered, but Meribah is a distinct named site with its own cause-and-effect clause, not a continuation of the Baal Peor plague and Phinehas's act.
observed_substrate_signals: the place name Meribah opens the episode at v32, the recital's fourth specific rebellion-site naming after Egypt/the Red Sea, Horeb, and Baal Peor
Moses is named as the one troubled, rather than as intercessor, a role reversal from v23's 'stood in the breach'
the episode's two verses form one cause-and-effect clause, unlike the multi-verse episodes surrounding it

edited_rows.rationale: The recital shifts from narrated deeds to Yahweh's own response, summarizing a repeated cycle rather than one episode: “Therefore Yahweh burned with anger against his people. He abhorred his inheritance.” (web:Ps.106.40) opens the cycle — subjection to the nations (web:Ps.106.41-Ps.106.42), repeated rescue answered by repeated rebellion, “He rescued them many times, but they were rebellious in their counsel, and were brought low in their iniquity.” (web:Ps.106.43) — the Hebrew adversative וְ֭הֵמָּה ('but they', oshb:Ps.106.43) marks the cycle's actual contrastive pivot, not the English 'Nevertheless' introduced by WEB's rendering of the wayyiqtol that follows at “Nevertheless he regarded their distress, when he heard their cry.” (web:Ps.106.44), וַ֭יַּרְא (oshb:Ps.106.44), which opens with a bare waw-consecutive and carries no MT adversative of its own; covenant remembrance, וַיִּזְכֹּ֣ר לָהֶ֣ם בְּרִית֑וֹ (oshb:Ps.106.45) (the verse carries a ketiv/qere pair, חסדו (oshb:Ps.106.45) ketiv against חֲסָדָֽיו (oshb:Ps.106.45) qere, at the same ref), and compassion before captors (web:Ps.106.46), before the recital's own voice returns to direct petition.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the anger-and-subjection verses (106:40-43) from the mercy-and-remembrance verses (106:44-46) into two rows was considered, but the adversative at v44 answers the very cycle the anger-and-subjection verses narrate, within one summarizing movement rather than two separate episodes.
observed_substrate_signals: the Hebrew adversative וְ֭הֵמָּה ('but they', oshb:Ps.106.43) marks the cycle's actual contrastive pivot; the English 'Nevertheless' at 106:44 and 106:8 (oshb:Ps.106.8, oshb:Ps.106.44) is WEB's rendering of a bare waw-consecutive at each verse, not a shared MT particle
a ketiv (unpointed) stands against a qere (pointed, 'his loving kindnesses') at v45 — the psalm's ketiv/qere pair, per the inventory
the verb sequence at v43 compresses the whole preceding recital's rescue-then-rebellion pattern into one summary verse

edited_rows.rationale: The recital's voice returns to direct petition, echoing the individual plea that opened the psalm: “Save us, Yahweh, our God, gather us from among the nations, to give thanks to your holy name, to triumph in your praise!” (web:Ps.106.47) — הוֹשִׁיעֵ֨נוּ יְה֘וָ֤ה אֱלֹהֵ֗ינוּ וְקַבְּצֵנוּ֮ (oshb:Ps.106.47). The imperative here is singular with a first-person-plural object suffix (הוֹשִׁיעֵ֨נוּ (oshb:Ps.106.47), 'save us'), structurally matching the singular imperative-plus-suffix pattern of the plea at 106:4, the contrast lying in the suffix's number (1cs 'me' vs. 1cp 'us') rather than the imperative's own form (זָכְרֵ֣נִי (oshb:Ps.106.4), 'remember me'); לְ֭הֹדוֹת (oshb:Ps.106.47) ('to give thanks') echoes the psalm's own opening (הוֹד֣וּ (oshb:Ps.106.1), 'give thanks') at v1. The psalm's own closing doxology follows with a blessing formula rather than continuing this petition.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Grouping 106:47 with the doxology of 106:48 as one closing unit was considered, but the plea's imperative petition and the doxology's fixed baruch-formula belong to different discourse types — request versus benediction — and the coda class is reserved for the fixed formula alone.
observed_substrate_signals: a plural imperative-suffix verb ('save us') echoes the singular ('remember me') of v4 in form (imperative plus pronominal suffix) while inverting its number
'to give thanks' at v47 verbally echoes the psalm's own opening 'give thanks' at v1
the plea closes with no book-boundary formula of its own; the doxology proper occupies the following verse

edited_rows.rationale: The psalm — and Book IV (Psalms 90-106) — closes on the fixed book-boundary doxology: “Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, from everlasting even to everlasting! Let all the people say, "Amen." Praise Yah!” (web:Ps.106.48) — בָּר֤וּךְ יְהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהֵ֪י יִשְׂרָאֵ֡ל מִן הָ֤עוֹלָ֨ם וְעַ֬ד הָעוֹלָ֗ם וְאָמַ֖ר כָּל הָעָ֥ם אָמֵ֗ן הַֽלְלוּ יָֽהּ (oshb:Ps.106.48). The verse carries one baruch clause, one amen, and the hallelu-Yah exclamation, הַֽלְלוּ יָֽהּ (oshb:Ps.106.48), that answers the psalm's own opening (הַֽלְלוּ יָ֨הּ (oshb:Ps.106.1)), closing the frame the psalm's own opening verse announced. The formula shares its class with the book's other book-boundary doxologies, but hallelu-Yah closes this one, and the amen count differs too: the book's other 3 book-boundary doxologies each carry 2 amens (41:13, 72:19, 89:52) and close without hallelu-Yah, against 1 amen here, per the inventory.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Folding 106:48 into the preceding petition as its closing line was considered, but the baruch-plus-amen-plus-hallelu-Yah formula shares its closing class with the book's other book-boundary doxologies rather than continuing the petition's own second-person request.
observed_substrate_signals: a baruch + amen x1 + hallelu-Yah formula matches, in class, the book I, II, and III closing doxologies (each baruch + amen x2, without hallelu-Yah)
the closing hallelu-Yah echoes the hallelu-Yah that opens v1, completing the frame the psalm announced at its own start
the doxology stands outside the petition's own second-person request, matching the book-boundary class rather than resolving the plea's content

edited_rows.rationale: The wilderness company: “They wandered in the wilderness in a desert way. They found no city to live in.” (web:Ps.107.4), “Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted in them.” (web:Ps.107.5). Their plight closes on the cry-refrain “וַיִּצְעֲק֣וּ אֶל יְ֭הוָה בַּצַּ֣ר לָהֶ֑ם” (oshb:Ps.107.6) -- "they cried to Yahweh in their trouble" -- spelled with tsade; deliverance follows at “He led them also by a straight way, that they might go to a city to live in.” (web:Ps.107.7), and the vignette closes on the yodu-refrain “יוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה חַסְדּ֑וֹ וְ֝נִפְלְאוֹתָ֗יו לִבְנֵ֥י אָדָֽם” (oshb:Ps.107.8): "let them praise Yahweh for his loving kindness, for his wonderful deeds to the children of men," plus a motive clause at “For he satisfies the longing soul. He fills the hungry soul with good.” (web:Ps.107.9). This plight-cry-deliverance-praise sequence, bounded by the two refrains (oshb:Ps.107.6, oshb:Ps.107.8), forms one recurring vignette pattern; three further companies repeat it through web:Ps.107.32.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the plight (4-5) from the cry-deliverance-praise sequence (6-9) into two rows was considered, but no refrain or discourse marker separates them -- the cry-refrain itself is the seam the vignette lattice recognizes, not a break inside the vignette.
observed_substrate_signals: cry-refrain, tsade spelling: וַיִּצְעֲק֣וּ אֶל יְ֭הוָה בַּצַּ֣ר לָהֶ֑ם (oshb:Ps.107.6)
yodu-refrain byte-quoted at oshb:Ps.107.8; recurs 4 times total across the vignette lattice, once per company closing it
edited_rows.device_notes: The four rescue-vignettes (107:4-9, 10-16, 17-22, 23-32) share a double refrain: a cry-to-Yahweh formula whose sibilant root changes by company, and a yodu-praise formula that returns byte-identical at each vignette's close (sweep: 4 of 4 returns byte tier).

edited_rows.rationale: A distinct company opens without transition: “Some sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, being bound in affliction and iron,” (web:Ps.107.10), with cause given at “because they rebelled against the words of God, and condemned the counsel of the Most High.” (web:Ps.107.11) and “Therefore he brought down their heart with labor. They fell down, and there was no one to help.” (web:Ps.107.12). The cry-refrain returns at “וַיִּזְעֲק֣וּ אֶל יְ֭הוָה בַּצַּ֣ר לָהֶ֑ם” (oshb:Ps.107.13), now spelled with zayin rather than the tsade of the wilderness company's cry (oshb:Ps.107.6) -- the four cry-openers run tsade-zayin-zayin-tsade across the lattice (an ABBA frame, not a strict alternation) rather than repeating one fixed spelling. Deliverance follows at “He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and broke away their chains.” (web:Ps.107.14), and the yodu-refrain opens the close at “יוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה חַסְדּ֑וֹ” (oshb:Ps.107.15), continuing to match oshb:Ps.107.8 at byte tier, with a further motive clause at “For he has broken the gates of bronze, and cut through bars of iron.” (web:Ps.107.16).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Treating 107:9 and 107:10 as one continuous unit was considered since neither carries an explicit conjunction, but 107:9 completes the wilderness company's own motive clause after its yodu-refrain, and 107:10 opens an unrelated company (those seated in darkness) with its own cry-and-yodu pair.
observed_substrate_signals: cry-refrain, zayin spelling: וַיִּזְעֲק֣וּ אֶל יְ֭הוָה בַּצַּ֣ר לָהֶ֑ם (oshb:Ps.107.13), against tsade at oshb:Ps.107.6
yodu-refrain opening tokens יוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה חַסְדּ֑וֹ match oshb:Ps.107.8 at byte tier

edited_rows.rationale: The seafarers' company opens “Those who go down to the sea in ships, who do business in great waters,” (web:Ps.107.23), “these see Yahweh's deeds, and his wonders in the deep.” (web:Ps.107.24), then the storm at “For he commands, and raises the stormy wind, which lifts up its waves.” (web:Ps.107.25) through “They reel back and forth, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits' end.” (web:Ps.107.27) -- 107:25 opens with the waw-prefixed narrative form 'וַיֹּ֗אמֶר' (oshb:Ps.107.25), continuing the storm narration from 107:24's "wonders" (WEB's own 'For' at 107:25 has no MT causal counterpart), so no seam separates the setting from the storm. The cry-refrain returns at “וַיִּצְעֲק֣וּ אֶל יְ֭הוָה בַּצַּ֣ר לָהֶ֑ם” (oshb:Ps.107.28), tsade-spelled like the wilderness company's cry (oshb:Ps.107.6) rather than the two zayin-spelled cries between them (oshb:Ps.107.13, oshb:Ps.107.19) -- the lattice runs tsade-zayin-zayin-tsade across the four companies, not a strict alternation. Calm follows at “He makes the storm a calm, so that its waves are still.” (web:Ps.107.29) and “Then they are glad because it is calm, so he brings them to their desired haven.” (web:Ps.107.30); the remaining 3 of the book's 7 inverted-nun segs fall inside this row (reversednun inventory: oshb:Ps.107.23, oshb:Ps.107.24, oshb:Ps.107.25, single-witness). The yodu-refrain closes at “יוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה חַסְדּ֑וֹ” (oshb:Ps.107.31), and the company's own response follows at “Let them exalt him also in the assembly of the people, and praise him in the seat of the elders.” (web:Ps.107.32).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting this row at 107:27|28 to keep the storm-plight (23-27) apart from the cry-deliverance-praise sequence (28-32), matching the companies at 107:4-9, 10-16, and 17-22, was considered; it would keep every vignette row under 8 verses, but the cry-refrain restart at 107:28 (a wayyiqtol after the non-waw plight verses 107:26-27) is the same formal marker that opens the cry-refrain internally, not at a row boundary, inside every other company (107:5|6, 107:18|19), so the row follows the vignette lattice as one unit.
observed_substrate_signals: cry-refrain, tsade spelling, matching oshb:Ps.107.6 at byte tier: וַיִּצְעֲק֣וּ אֶל יְ֭הוָה בַּצַּ֣ר לָהֶ֑ם; the four cries run tsade-zayin-zayin-tsade, not simple alternation

inverted-nun segs at oshb:Ps.107.23-25 (3 more of 7 book-wide; together with the 3 at 107:20-22 disclosed at 107:17-22, 6 of 7 are now accounted for, leaving MT 107:39 as the sole seg still outstanding)

edited_rows.rationale: After the vignette lattice's fourth refrain closes, the psalm turns to an unrefrained hymn: “He turns rivers into a desert, water springs into a thirsty ground,” (web:Ps.107.33), “and a fruitful land into a salt waste, for the wickedness of those who dwell in it.” (web:Ps.107.34) -- fertile land turned to waste for its inhabitants' wickedness. The verb “יָשֵׂ֣ם” (oshb:Ps.107.33) recurs verse-initial, matching at byte tier, at “יָשֵׂ֣ם” (oshb:Ps.107.35), reversing the direction: “He turns a desert into a pool of water, and a dry land into water springs.” (web:Ps.107.35), “There he makes the hungry live, that they may prepare a city to live in,” (web:Ps.107.36), “sow fields, plant vineyards, and reap the fruits of increase.” (web:Ps.107.37), “He blesses them also, so that they are multiplied greatly. He doesn't allow their livestock to decrease.” (web:Ps.107.38). No cry-refrain or yodu-refrain marks this unit's edges; the seam at 107:32|33 rests on the shift from the fourth company's own response clause to this paired judgment-then-blessing hymn, not on a formulaic return.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Reading 107:33-43 as one eleven-verse coda was considered; this row instead closes at 107:38, at the reversal-of-reversal pivot beginning 107:39 -- though the waw-prefixed narrative chain runs unbroken from 107:36 through 107:39 (broken only at 107:40's non-waw opener), a grammatical continuity signal disclosed here rather than overriding the content-based split.
observed_substrate_signals: verb יָשֵׂ֣ם repeats verse-initial at oshb:Ps.107.33 and oshb:Ps.107.35, matching at byte tier, marking a judgment/blessing pair rather than a refrain return
no cry-refrain or yodu-refrain token in 107:33-38 (absence relative to the refrain lattice earlier in the psalm)
edited_rows.device_notes: Whether 107:33-43 is one wisdom-coda or two internally distinct movements is the psalm's real open seam question; the span here splits it at 107:38|39 on the reversal-of-reversal pivot ("again, they are diminished," 107:39) rather than reading it as one undivided close.

edited_rows.rationale: The blessing of 107:35-38 reverses again: “וַיִּמְעֲט֥וּ וַיָּשֹׁ֑חוּ” (oshb:Ps.107.39) -- 'they diminish and are bowed down' -- opens “Again, they are diminished and bowed down through oppression, trouble, and sorrow.” (web:Ps.107.39); the book's 7th and final inverted-nun seg falls here (reversednun inventory: oshb:Ps.107.39, single-witness, seg layer, not quotable as verse bytes). Oppressors are humbled at “He pours contempt on princes, and causes them to wander in a trackless waste.” (web:Ps.107.40) while the needy are lifted at “Yet he lifts the needy out of their affliction, and increases their families like a flock.” (web:Ps.107.41); onlookers react at “The upright will see it, and be glad. All the wicked will shut their mouths.” (web:Ps.107.42). The psalm closes on a wisdom maxim addressed past the narrative entirely: “מִי חָכָ֥ם” (oshb:Ps.107.43) -- "whoever is wise" -- “Whoever is wise will pay attention to these things. They will consider the loving kindnesses of Yahweh.” (web:Ps.107.43), a register no earlier verse of this psalm uses.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Closing the span at 107:38 instead of 107:39, so this row would instead run 107:40-43, was considered; the waw-prefixed narrative chain runs unbroken from 107:36 through 107:39 (broken only at 107:40), a grammatical continuity signal disclosed here, but 107:39's own reversal ('they diminish and are bowed down') is the content pivot away from 107:35-38's blessing, not a continuation of it, so it opens this row rather than closing the span before it.
observed_substrate_signals: reversal-opening token וַיִּמְעֲט֥וּ וַיָּשֹׁ֑חוּ (oshb:Ps.107.39, 'they diminish and are bowed down') pivots away from 107:38's blessing
closing wisdom-maxim formula מִי חָכָ֥ם (oshb:Ps.107.43) is a register found nowhere else in Psalm 107 (sweep: 1 of 43 verses)
inverted-nun seg at oshb:Ps.107.39 (the final one of the book's 7, single-witness)
